doc.title: Dorothy Donegan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The wartime entertainment tax and her wiggling at the piano
summary: A tax claim on her wiggling was settled by the union as long as she kept playing; she says critics were women pianists with flat behinds.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Can you tell me about the wartime entertainment tax against entertainers? 20% tax on entertainers during the war years.

I don’t remember that. Unless it was on me. They claimed that I wiggled when I played and there should be a tax on it, you know. So the union says, “Well, she can wiggle as long as she keeps playing the piano.” Some of the women pianists were kind of jealous.
Did that get you off the hook and keep you categorized as a musician?
Oh yeah. And one of the owners said, “My wife don’t want to come in here since she’s here.” I said, “I know she don’t mind spending the money I made.”
Tell me about the wiggling, the hip shaking, the arm flourishes.

I’d be playing and I’d be wiggling and most people wanted to sit in the back rather than in the front. So people like the Duke and Duchess of Windsor would come in, Tallulah Bankhead, Ronald Reagan and his wife, Robert Montgomery and his wife, they all want to see me.
When did some of those aspects become a part of your performance style?
I guess during then. Of course I don’t do it as much now, I don’t have the energy. And I find, the more piano playing you do, you don’t have to do that.
Were you ever criticized for that?
Yes, some people criticized it, you know. So I said, “Well, as long as I play the piano, I can shake. Some people don’t have nothing to shake.”
Who would criticize you for that?
Why is that? Did they not have something to shake?
No, their behind was kind of flat.
